narrative:
The 2017 Washington Nationals arrived with championship expectations, and for the most part they delivered a season worthy of the hype. Behind a rotation anchored by Max Scherzer and Stephen Strasburg, and an offense powered by Bryce Harper and a surprisingly productive supporting cast, Washington raced out of the gate with a 17-8 April — the franchise's best start in years. Harper's three-run blast on April 16th, worth nearly 0.81 WPA, announced that the Nationals were ready to be taken seriously as World Series contenders.

The middle months brought the inevitable turbulence of a 162-game season. The bullpen — long Washington's Achilles' heel — flashed its vulnerability through May and June, with Enny Romero, Matt Albers, Koda Glover, and Blake Treinen all contributing costly meltdowns. A brutal June went 14-14, the one month that threatened to derail the season's promise. Yet the Nationals never truly slipped, and a scorching 16-8 July followed by an 18-11 August reaffirmed their standing atop the NL East. Even on the nights when the bullpen gave games away, the offense — led by Harper, Adam Lind, and the steady Anthony Rendon — found ways to keep winning.

The postseason arrived with the Nationals hosting the Chicago Cubs in the NLDS, and what followed was a series of breathtaking highs and crushing lows compressed into five unforgettable games. Ryan Zimmerman's three-run homer and Harper's solo shot in Game 2 gave Washington momentum, and Michael A. Taylor's grand slam in Game 4 at Nationals Park seemed to set up a decisive Game 5. But in the deciding game, the Cubs chipped away against Scherzer, and the Nationals' offense — so potent all season — fell silent at the worst moment.

In the end, the 2017 Nationals finished 97-65, one of the best records in franchise history, only to join the long list of Washington squads that could not break through in October. The talent was undeniable — the pitching elite, the lineup deep, the individual moments spectacular. But postseason baseball has a cruel math, and for the fourth time in seven years, the Nationals' season ended in the division round, leaving a city to wonder what might have been.

chapters.title: Hot Out of the Gate
chapters.description: Washington posts a blistering 17-8 April, with Bryce Harper's mammoth three-run home run serving as the season's early exclamation point.

chapters.title: Bullpen Cracks, Bats Answer
chapters.description: May brings a mixed bag as the bullpen hemorrhages key leads, but clutch hits from Harper, Wieters, and Michael A. Taylor keep Washington afloat at 16-11.

chapters.title: The June Wobble
chapters.description: A 14-14 June exposes the team's bullpen fragility, with costly late-inning collapses against Texas, Atlanta, and Miami threatening to stall the season's momentum.

chapters.title: Surging to the NL East Crown
chapters.description: Washington shakes off its midsummer struggles with a dominant July-August stretch, going 34-19 to lock up the division title despite continued bullpen hiccups.

chapters.title: October Heartbreak
chapters.description: The Nationals battle the Cubs in a thrilling five-game NLDS, with Michael A. Taylor's grand slam and Harper's homer unable to prevent a gut-wrenching elimination in Game 5.
